question: How do power-law input statistics, teacher anisotropy, initialization, and mode-dependent learning jointly reshape the eigenspectrum of a network's internal representation over training?

key_findings.claim: The hidden-representation spectrum has an exact decomposition into input-inherited and teacher-induced components in the solvable model.
key_findings.evidence: For a wide two-layer linear student with aligned input and teacher eigenspaces, the representation eigenvalue is rho_k(t)=lambda_k sigma_w^2+lambda_k Delta eta_k(t). The first term is fixed at initialization and the second is formed through joint layer learning; eigenvalue rank ordering is preserved over time.

key_findings.claim: Feature learning can create four distinct local power-law slopes across mode-time domains.
key_findings.evidence: Away from transition boundaries, the derived effective exponent takes alpha in the initialization-dominated region, 3 alpha + beta for newly learning modes dominated by the learned component, alpha + beta when learned deformation is primarily in the first layer, and alpha + beta/2 when both layers participate.

key_findings.claim: A fixed mode's anisotropy changes nonmonotonically because modes learn at different rates.
key_findings.evidence: In the feature-learning regime, a mode can progress from alpha to 3 alpha + beta and then relax to alpha + beta or alpha + beta/2. The early transient steepening comes from the lambda_k-dependent learning timescale, followed by incorporation of teacher structure and redistribution of learning across layers.

key_findings.claim: Lazy training preserves the input spectrum rather than forming the multi-regime deformation.
key_findings.evidence: When gamma_0 is small enough that the learned term never overtakes the initialization term, R_k remains much less than one for every mode, so rho_k stays approximately sigma_w^2 lambda_k and the effective exponent remains alpha.

key_findings.claim: The main spectral transition survives in a finite nonlinear ReLU student under the paper's synthetic teacher-student setup.
key_findings.evidence: With D=P=512, width 8192, and 4096 fixed samples, the feature-learning run shows mode-by-mode slope evolution from alpha toward alpha + beta, while the lazy run stays near alpha; spectra are measured from hidden preactivations.

method.core_idea: Solve hidden-representation covariance dynamics mode by mode in a wide two-layer linear teacher-student model with aligned power-law input and teacher spectra, then classify the local slopes by which component and layer-learning regime dominates.
method.mechanism: Take hidden width to infinity with equal finite input and output dimension, train both factorized linear layers by population gradient flow, use simultaneous diagonalization to decouple modes, solve the Gram-matrix dynamics exactly, and define three dimensionless ratios that mark input-versus-learned dominance, learned-versus-unlearned modes, and first-layer-versus-both-layer allocation. Validate the predicted slope changes in finite linear and ReLU networks.
assumptions: Input covariance and teacher Gram matrix are simultaneously diagonalizable and both have exact power-law eigenvalues over the studied mode range.
Input and output dimensions are equal and much smaller than infinite hidden width; broad spectral evolution may not occur when output dimension is much smaller than input dimension.
Training follows population-limit gradient flow on mean-squared error with Gaussian initialization.
Asymptotic exponents describe domains sufficiently far from boundaries; boundary regions need not follow one power law.
The nonlinear validation uses the same synthetic aligned teacher-student structure and does not establish behavior on natural data or large language models.

techniques.role: Uses aligned eigenspaces to reduce matrix gradient flow to independent scalar mode equations.
Separates the hidden covariance into input-inherited variance and a teacher-induced training increment.
Defines a mode- and time-dependent effective exponent instead of fitting one global power law.
Uses dominance, learning-progress, and layer-allocation ratios to derive asymptotic regions and their boundaries.
Eliminates coupled layer variables and yields a closed exact solution for the representation eigenvalues.

evaluations.setting: Finite two-layer linear network with D=P=512, width 8192, 4096 fixed Gaussian samples, alpha=beta=1
evaluations.result: Numerical eigenvalue trajectories closely follow the analytical solution and show the predicted changing local slope

evaluations.setting: Two-layer ReLU student with the same D, P, width, sample count, input spectrum, and teacher
evaluations.result: Feature-learning initialization changes the slope from alpha toward alpha+beta over learned modes, while lazy initialization remains near alpha
evaluations.baseline: Lazy-regime ReLU student and the linear-theory prediction

limitations: Author-stated: the theory requires simultaneous diagonalizability of input covariance and teacher structure.
Author-stated: the exact result assumes infinite width, infinite data, and gradient flow.
Author-stated: extensions to misalignment, finite width and samples, deeper networks, and general nonlinear activations remain open.
Author-stated: it is unknown how clearly the predicted domains and boundaries appear in real data and large-scale models.
Reviewer-identified: the nonlinear evidence consists of one synthetic ReLU configuration and demonstrates only the main alpha-to-alpha+beta transition, not all four asymptotic regimes.
Reviewer-identified: equal input-output dimension is atypical for many classification and regression tasks and is explicitly needed for evolution over a broad mode range.
failure_modes: Misaligned teacher and input eigenvectors couple modes, invalidating the independent-mode solution and possibly changing rank order.
Near cross, learn, or layer boundaries, the spectrum interpolates continuously and a single fitted slope can be misleading.
Finite data can corrupt tail eigenvalues and make local exponents dominated by sampling noise.
If the learned component never exceeds initialization, the proposed multi-regime signature is absent even though output learning occurs.
A narrow output bottleneck prevents teacher-induced changes across most input modes.
Global power-law fits can average broken or time-varying domains into a spurious single exponent.
reusable_insights: Decompose representation spectra into inherited data geometry and task-induced change before attributing a power law to learning.
Estimate local slopes over mode bands and training time rather than reporting one exponent for an entire spectrum.
Use dimensionless ratios to identify which mechanism dominates before applying an asymptotic approximation.
Mode-dependent learning times alone can transiently steepen an eigenspectrum before the final task geometry emerges.
Layer-balance initialization controls not only optimization speed but how learned anisotropy is allocated across layers.
open_questions: How does eigenvector misalignment alter the exponent domains when modes no longer decouple?
Which finite-sample estimators can reliably detect moving local slopes in the noisy spectral tail?
Do transformers show analogous mode-time boundaries during pretraining and post-training?
Can task-induced spectral deformation predict transfer, robustness, or generalization better than a static exponent near one?
How do depth, residual connections, and normalization alter the alpha+beta versus alpha+beta/2 layer-allocation result?
Can one infer teacher anisotropy or learning regime from observed spectral trajectories alone?

competitive_landscape.title: Exact solutions to the nonlinear dynamics of learning in deep linear neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Saxe et al. derive exact stage-like learning dynamics and mode learning times in deep linear networks. This paper specializes the dynamics to aligned power-law input and teacher spectra and derives the evolving hidden-covariance exponent and its four local domains.

competitive_landscape.title: From Lazy to Rich: Exact Learning Dynamics in Deep Linear Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Dominé et al. solve representation and neural-tangent-kernel evolution across rich and lazy regimes under lambda-balanced initializations, with continual and transfer applications. This paper instead asks how aligned power-law anisotropy changes across mode and time and provides explicit exponent formulas and boundaries.

competitive_landscape.title: Investigating Power laws in Deep Representation Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Ghosh et al. empirically fit feature-covariance power laws across supervised and self-supervised vision models and relate exponents near one to downstream quality. This paper gives a mechanistic training-time theory showing that a representation may have several local exponents rather than one fixed fit.

competitive_landscape.title: A Dynamical Model of Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.difference: Bordelon et al. use a solvable random-feature model to explain performance scaling with time, data, and width. This paper studies hidden-representation geometry under feature learning, including teacher-induced spectral deformation that a fixed random-feature kernel does not capture.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: this is the first exact characterization of how the local power-law exponent of an internal representation evolves during learning, including up to four asymptotic values and a feature-learning versus lazy split. Prior work already supplies exact deep-linear learning dynamics, exact rich-to-lazy representation dynamics, empirical power-law representation studies, and power-law kernel scaling theories. Reviewer inference: the novel piece is the synthesis of aligned power-law input and teacher structure with exact mode dynamics to obtain explicit moving exponent domains; the general facts that deep-linear modes learn stagewise and rich learning changes representations are established. External validity is currently limited by the aligned synthetic setting.
reviewer_notes: The four formulas and regime conditions were checked against pages 6-9 and Appendices D-F. The ReLU numerical dimensions and parameters were checked on page 26. Competitive differences were verified against primary arXiv and OpenReview records.
